clue.text: Time for a drink with boy on the blower

parts.note: rum is a spirit, a drink
Peter is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Someone takes a break for a drink with a lad while chatting on the telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the blower' is British slang for being on the phone; here it means playing a blown instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of a brass instrument blows into it, so such a musician is literally on a blower.

clue.text: Inexhaustible novel takes in country and leaves

indicators.note: a word that takes in another holds it inside itself

parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Hardy's novel, often just Tess

indicators.note: when the word 'and' leaves, it is taken away from the country's name

parts.note: Ireland is a country
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tireless book that ranges over a nation and its foliage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like foliage but is a verb meaning departs; 'takes in' signals the insertion. Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Thomas Hardy's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tireless never tires, so is inexhaustible.

clue.text: Not from the country of original Prohibition

parts.note: Ur- is a prefix meaning original or primitive, as in Urtext
a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: A city-dweller with no link to the place where Prohibition first began.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes towns and cities, the opposite of rural, so not of the countryside.

clue.text: Risk from others I don't know, with saint a short time on the throne

parts.note: in a quiz, 'pass' is what you say when you don't know the answer
St Ives is named after a saint, Ives
mo is short for moment
a king sits on the throne

explanation.surface: Someone unsure of their place reflects on a saint's brief reign.
explanation.walkthrough: St Ives, the Cornish town, takes its name from a saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Breathing in others' tobacco smoke is a health hazard caused by other people.

clue.text: Beginning of concession to limited working of the mind

parts.note: a concessive clause typically begins with 'though'

indicators.note: a word that is limited is cut short, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A grudging start to a compromise with a narrow mind at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning of concession' looks like it wants a first letter, C, but means the word that opens a concessive clause.
explanation.definitionFit: Thought is the process of thinking, the mind at work.

clue.text: There's jolly good beer up at the Crown etc

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: A1, written AI, means first-rate
lager is a beer

explanation.surface: A pub called the Crown serves excellent beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns AILAGER round; the surface makes 'the Crown' sound like a pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: Regalia are the emblems of royalty such as crown, sceptre and orb.

clue.text: Just stalls and amusements

explanation.definitionFit: Just means equitable or even-handed; a funfair is a gathering of stalls, rides and amusements.

clue.text: Terrible liar with interminable vanity makes treatment for Aids

indicators.note: something terrible is in a dreadful state, so its letters are rearranged
interminable here means without its end, losing the last letter

explanation.surface: A dreadful conceited fibber somehow produces a medicine for Aids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interminable' cuts VANITY to VANIT; 'Terrible' rearranges LIAR plus VANIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiviral drugs act against viruses such as HIV, which causes Aids.

clue.text: News of the Bang?

explanation.walkthrough: A report is an account of news, and also the sound of an explosion or gunshot.
explanation.definitionFit: A news account is called this, and so is the loud noise of a gun or explosion.

clue.text: Three thousand, unharmed, to be knocked down

annotationWithheld.why: Three thousand, unharmed, to be knocked down: anagram of THREE + M + UNHARMED, but the only indicator is 'knocked down', which is also the definition 'to be knocked down' (word doing two jobs)
annotationWithheld.clue: Three thousand, unharmed, to be knocked down

clue.text: Fictional sleuth dealing with transport

parts.note: re means concerning, about, dealing with
a bus is a means of transport

explanation.surface: A detective in a novel who works on transport cases.
explanation.walkthrough: John Rebus is the Edinburgh detective in Ian Rankin's crime novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Rebus is the detective hero of Ian Rankin's series of crime novels.

clue.text: Cardiac arrest? Pull out every one like this

definitions.text: Pull out every one like this

explanation.walkthrough: The heart is an organ, so its stopping is cryptically an organ's stop; and to pull out all the stops is to use every one of an organ's controls.
explanation.definitionFit: Heart failure read literally is an organ halting, and the idiom 'pull out all the stops' refers to the knobs on a church instrument.

clue.text: School releasing septic matter?

explanation.walkthrough: Lancing College is a well-known English independent school in West Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancing College is an English public school; lancing a boil pierces it so that pus drains out.

clue.text: Be left till next meeting — when truth will be told at last?

definitions.text: when truth will be told at last?

explanation.walkthrough: Business that is postponed is said to lie over; read whimsically, the phrase says the lying is over, so the truth comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie over is to be deferred to a later session; humorously it means the telling of falsehoods has finished.

clue.text: Expose the less glossy? That's what it's all about

parts.note: to subject someone to something is to expose them to it
matter, as in more matt, is a comparative meaning less shiny

explanation.surface: A question about revealing the duller parts, with a reply about the point of it all.
explanation.walkthrough: MATTER is read as the comparative of 'matt', a dull non-glossy finish.
explanation.definitionFit: The topic or theme of a work is what that work is about.

clue.text: Pirate queen supports rising youngster getting the stick

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the others
in a down entry, rising means read upwards

parts.note: a cub is a youngster, a young animal or junior scout
a cane is a stick, used for punishment
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A queen props up a child who is about to be beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' turns CUB to BUC; 'supports' puts ER below the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer is a sea-robber, especially of the old Caribbean.

clue.text: Supporter of church embraced by tennis player

indicators.note: a piece embraced by another is held inside it

parts.note: Tim Henman, British tennis player

explanation.surface: A churchgoing fan is hugged by a tennis star.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim Henman was Britain's leading men's tennis player around 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: A henchman is a loyal follower or backer, a sidekick.

clue.text: Representative of university, the lighter one

explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is someone who has represented Oxford or Cambridge at sport; Cambridge's colour is a paler shade than Oxford's dark blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A sportsperson awarded colours by the Fenland university is so called, and that university's shade is lighter than Oxford's.

clue.text: Artist to draw life as competition

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is an artist
to trace is to draw over an outline

explanation.surface: A painter sets out to draw life as a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the relentless competitive struggle of modern working life.

clue.text: Change direction of student engulfed by flaw

indicators.note: a piece engulfed by another is swallowed up inside it

parts.note: a defect is a flaw
L is a learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A student swamped by a fault changes course.
explanation.definitionFit: To deflect something is to turn it aside from its course.

clue.text: Online remarks about Pole following round figure

indicators.note: the second piece follows the first

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: a piece placed about another surrounds it

parts.note: a blog is a set of online posts
N is the North Pole

explanation.surface: Internet comments about a Polish person after a round number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' is a magnetic pole, N, not a person from Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblong is a rectangle, a geometric figure.

clue.text: Cover for audience, dash it!

indicators.note: something put on for an audience is heard rather than read, so the sound of the next words counts

parts.note: 'blank it' is a mild euphemistic curse, like 'dash it' or 'blast it'

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in irritation while hunting for a cover for the spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash it' and 'blank it' are both genteel stand-ins for a stronger oath.
explanation.definitionFit: A woollen bed covering, and more generally any covering layer, as in a blanket of snow.

clue.text: Craft in trouble makes one distraught

indicators.note: trouble here is a disturbance that throws these letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A boat in difficulty leaves its sailor very upset.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone distraught is wild with worry or grief, desperately agitated.

clue.text: Sit on gate, no location for friendly country

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letters are taken away

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken in these words by coincidence; the setter's device is taking out the letters of the location
a site is a location

explanation.surface: Someone straddles a fence, unsure where a welcoming nation is.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove S, I and T, E from SITONGATE. Tonga was called the Friendly Islands by Captain Cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is known as the Friendly Islands, a name given by Cook.

clue.text: Used once, a greeting on which a life is celebrated

definitions.text: on which a life is celebrated

indicators.note: letters that are used have been worked over and so are rearranged here

parts.note: taken as written
a wave of the hand is a greeting

explanation.surface: A salutation once employed at a celebration of someone's life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used' rearranges ONCE A to give OCEAN. The definition alludes to the song 'A Life on the Ocean Wave', the Royal Marines' march.
explanation.definitionFit: The song 'A Life on the Ocean Wave' celebrates a sailor's life lived upon the sea's billows.

clue.text: Drop a note?

explanation.walkthrough: In the old apothecaries' system a minim was a fluid measure of about one drop.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a tiny liquid measure roughly equal to a drop, and also a musical half note.

clue.text: Cover for boast from the right

indicators.note: reading from the right means taking the word backwards in an across clue

parts.note: brag means boast

explanation.surface: A disguise or cover story concocted for someone's showing off.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb is clothing, which covers the body.

clue.text: Consider how to give a party?

explanation.walkthrough: To entertain an idea is to consider it; to entertain guests is to host them.
explanation.definitionFit: Entertaining a proposal means considering it, and entertaining friends means hosting them at a gathering.
